intro: In this college you'll learn how to introduce yourself in Dutch: say your name, tell people where you come from, give your age and phone number, fill in a simple form, and greet your neighbours.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — and why this matters
paragraphs.text: Welcome to the very first theme of your Dutch course. Its title is [[Wie ben je?]], which means 'Who are you?'. Introducing yourself is the first thing you do in any language, and in the Netherlands you do it again and again: at the town hall, which is called the [[gemeente]]; at the doctor; at your children's school; and whenever you meet your neighbours. So although it feels basic, getting this right gives you confidence in every other situation. The two questions you will hear most often both mean 'what is your name?'. The informal one is [[Hoe heet je?]], and you will also hear [[Wat is je naam?]]. There is a polite version too: [[Hoe heet u?]]. Listen carefully for that small word [[u]], because it is the respectful way to speak to someone you do not know yet. In this college I explain everything in English, but every Dutch word and sentence you hear is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so you also train your ear and your pronunciation. Try to repeat each Dutch phrase out loud after me. Are you ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Saying your name: je or u?
paragraphs.text: Let's learn how to answer. You have three natural options. You can say [[Ik heet]] and then your name. You can say [[Mijn naam is]] and your name. Or you can simply say [[Ik ben]] and your name. For example: [[Ik heet Ayhan.]] Or: [[Mijn naam is Sara.]] Here is a quick pronunciation tip: the word [[mijn]] sounds a little like the English word 'mine', because the Dutch letters i-j are pronounced like 'eye'. Now, one of the most important ideas in all of Dutch is the difference between two little words: [[je]] and [[u]]. [[Je]] is informal — you use it with friends, family, children, and most people your own age. [[U]] is formal and polite — you use it with officials, with older people, and with anyone you want to show respect to. When you are not sure, start with [[u]]; it is never rude. So to a friend you might ask [[En jij, hoe heet jij?]], but to an official at a desk you would say [[En u, hoe heet u?]]. When Dutch people meet for the first time, they usually shake hands and say their own name, and a warm thing to add is [[Aangenaam!]], which means 'pleased to meet you'.

paragraphs.heading: Where are you from?
paragraphs.text: The next thing people ask is where you come from. The question is [[Waar kom je vandaan?]], which literally means 'where do you come from?'. You answer with [[Ik kom uit]] and the name of a country. For example: [[Ik kom uit Turkije.]] Or: [[Ik kom uit Syrië.]] To say where you live now, use [[Ik woon in]] and a city, like this: [[Ik woon in Rotterdam.]] You can also state your nationality with [[Ik ben]] and a nationality word, for example [[Ik ben Turks.]] People often ask about language too, with the question [[Welke talen spreek je?]] You answer with [[Ik spreek]] and your languages, for example: [[Ik spreek Turks, Engels en een beetje Nederlands.]] That last little phrase, [[een beetje Nederlands]], means 'a little Dutch', and it is one of the most useful things you can say in your first months, because it gently asks people to speak slowly and be patient with you. Notice the simple verb forms [[ik kom]], [[ik woon]] and [[ik spreek]]. In Dutch, the 'I' form of most verbs is just the short stem, so you can start making real sentences very quickly.

paragraphs.heading: Age, numbers and your phone number
paragraphs.text: This theme also introduces numbers, because you need them for your age and your phone number. To ask someone's age, you say [[Hoe oud ben je?]] You answer with [[Ik ben]], a number, and the word [[jaar]], for example [[Ik ben veertig jaar.]] Let's hear the numbers from zero to ten: [[nul, een, twee, drie, vier, vijf, zes, zeven, acht, negen, tien]]. And here are the tens: [[tien, twintig, dertig, veertig, vijftig]]. One thing surprises almost every learner: in Dutch you say the small number before the big one. So twenty-one is [[eenentwintig]], literally 'one-and-twenty', and thirty-five is [[vijfendertig]]. For a phone number, the question is [[Wat is je telefoonnummer?]], and you usually read the digits one by one. You will give your [[telefoonnummer]] very often — at the doctor, at the [[gemeente]], and in shops — so practise your own number out loud. And when someone speaks too quickly, this sentence is pure gold: [[Kunt u dat herhalen?]], which means 'can you repeat that?'. You can also ask [[Kunt u langzamer praten?]], 'can you speak more slowly?'. Never be afraid to use them.

paragraphs.heading: Filling in a form
paragraphs.text: A very practical part of this theme is filling in a form, which in Dutch is [[een formulier invullen]]. Forms are everywhere in the Netherlands, so you must recognise the standard fields. Your first name is your [[voornaam]], and your family name is your [[achternaam]]. Your date of birth is your [[geboortedatum]], and your place of birth is your [[geboorteplaats]]. Your address is your [[adres]], and it splits into the street, [[straat]]; the house number, [[huisnummer]]; the postal code, [[postcode]]; and the town where you live, [[woonplaats]]. You will also meet the word [[geslacht]], which means 'gender', with the options [[man]] and [[vrouw]], and the word [[nationaliteit]], your nationality. Many official forms also ask for your citizen service number, the [[burgerservicenummer]], usually shortened to B-S-N. Right at the bottom, a form almost always asks for your signature, your [[handtekening]], next to the date, the [[datum]]. If a clerk hands you a form and you feel unsure, this one sentence saves the day: [[Kunt u mij helpen met dit formulier?]], which means 'can you help me with this form?'.

paragraphs.heading: Greetings & meeting your neighbour
paragraphs.text: Finally, let's put it all together the way it really happens: greeting people. In the morning you say [[Goedemorgen]]. In the afternoon, [[Goedemiddag]]. And in the evening, [[Goedenavond]]. A simple [[Hallo]] or [[Hoi]] works any time with people you know. When you meet someone new, you can say [[Aangenaam]] or [[Leuk je te ontmoeten]] — both mean 'nice to meet you'. To say goodbye, use [[Tot ziens]], the casual [[Doei]], or [[Tot morgen]] if you will see them tomorrow. Now imagine a new neighbour knocks on your door. You could say: [[Hallo, ik ben uw nieuwe buurman.]] [[Ik heet Ayhan.]] [[Aangenaam!]] If you are a woman, you would say [[buurvrouw]] instead of [[buurman]]. That one little introduction opens the door to your whole neighbourhood. So practise it out loud today with your partner: greet each other, say your names, and ask where the other person comes from. In the coming themes we build directly on these blocks — shopping, the weather, the doctor — but it all begins with a confident hello. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — and I will see you in theme two!
